The Christian Church & Medieval Medicine

In the Middle Ages, the Christian Church was very powerful and controlled almost every part of life, including medicine. It ran the universities where doctors trained, decided which books could be studied, and shaped how ordinary people understood illness. The Church taught that God sent illness as a punishment for sin or as a test of faith.

Religious remedies — prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, and repentance — were often the first response to illness. However, the Church also provided the only organised care for the sick and poor in medieval Britain.

Medieval people also believed in miasma — the idea that “bad air” caused disease. Foul-smelling vapours from rotting matter, swamps, and sewage were thought to enter the body and make people ill. This belief lasted for centuries, influencing public health into the 19th century. During plague outbreaks, people carried posies of flowers or sweet herbs to ward off the “poisonous” air.

Medieval Hospitals

The Church was the main provider of hospital care in medieval Britain. By 1500, there were over 1,200 hospitals across the country. These were very different from modern hospitals — their purpose was to care for the sick, not cure them. Most were small and attached to monasteries or run by religious orders. Only around 10% actually cared for the sick. The rest offered “hospitality” in its original sense: a place to rest, eat, and pray, not receive medical treatment.

Key Fact — Medieval Hospitals
  • Run by monks, nuns, or religious orders — not trained doctors
  • Provided food, shelter, warmth, and prayer for the sick and poor
  • Rarely attempted to treat or cure diseases
  • Often refused entry to patients with infectious diseases to protect other residents
  • The focus was on spiritual care: patients were encouraged to pray and confess their sins

Monastery Sanitation

Monks had the knowledge, money, and discipline to create much better public health systems than towns had. Monasteries had excellent water supplies and built latrines to carry away sewage, keeping their water source separate from waste. They also had infirmaries for sick monks and herb gardens to grow plants for remedies.

This made monasteries some of the cleanest and healthiest places in medieval Britain. Regular washing, clean water, and organised waste disposal put them far ahead of most towns.

Monastery herb gardens were an important source of remedies. One example is foxglove, used to treat “feebleness of the heart.” A chemical from foxglove called digitalis is still used in modern medicine for heart conditions — one of the clearest examples of a medieval remedy with real scientific value.

The Church: Help or Hindrance?

A key exam theme is whether the Church helped or hindered medical progress. The answer is both — and examiners expect you to show this balance.

By 1300, there were fewer than 100 trained physicians in all of England. Most ordinary people could never afford one and instead relied on local healers, wise women, or the Church for their healthcare.

Roger Bacon, a 13th-century Franciscan friar, argued that doctors should carry out experiments rather than just relying on Galen. For challenging Church teaching, he was arrested and imprisoned — a clear warning to anyone who dared question accepted ideas.

Exam Tip

For questions about the Church’s role, you must give a balanced argument. Explain both the positive contributions and the negative effects. The strongest answers reach a judgement on whether the Church did more to help or hinder — and back it up with specific evidence.

Islamic Medicine

While Europe was in the “Dark Ages” after the fall of Rome, the Islamic world was in a golden age of learning. Islamic scholars translated, preserved, and built upon Greek and Roman medical texts — especially Hippocrates and Galen. Without them, much of this knowledge would have been lost forever.

The Islamic faith actively encouraged learning. The Quran taught that Muslims had a duty to care for the sick and seek cures. Medicine was valued and funded across the Islamic world, leading to major advances.

Rhazes (al-Razi, c.854–925 AD)

Rhazes (also known as al-Razi) was a Persian physician who made several breakthroughs. He was the first doctor to clearly distinguish between smallpox and measles — two diseases previously confused. He did this through careful clinical observation, recording each disease’s symptoms in detail.

Rhazes wrote over 200 medical texts and ran a hospital in Baghdad. He used clinical observation in the tradition of Hippocrates — carefully watching patients and recording symptoms rather than just relying on ancient texts.

Ibn Sina / Avicenna (c.980–1037 AD)

Ibn Sina (known in Europe as Avicenna) was perhaps the most influential Islamic physician. His masterwork, The Canon of Medicine, compiled and organised all known medical knowledge from the Greek, Roman, and Islamic traditions.

Key Fact — The Canon of Medicine

Ibn Sina’s Canon of Medicine was translated into Latin and became the standard medical textbook in European universities for over 500 years. It covered topics including the properties of drugs, the diagnosis and treatment of diseases, and the importance of diet, exercise, and hygiene. It contained descriptions of over 760 different drugs and their effects.

Ibn al-Nafis (c.1213–1288 AD)

Ibn al-Nafis was a Syrian physician who criticised Galen’s ideas about how blood moved through the body. Galen claimed blood was made in the liver, “burned up” by the organs, and passed between the two sides of the heart through invisible pores. Ibn al-Nafis rejected this. He correctly argued that blood circulated around the body and passed through the lungs — centuries before William Harvey proved full circulation in 1628.

Islamic Contributions to Pharmacy

Islamic scholars also made major advances in pharmacy. Through alchemy, they developed techniques like distillation to create purer, more effective medicines. They set up the first dedicated pharmacies and developed systems for testing and cataloguing drugs.

These advances fed back into European medicine when Islamic texts were translated into Latin, especially in Spain and Sicily. The knowledge Islamic scholars preserved and advanced was essential to the medical breakthroughs of the European Renaissance.

The Crusades & Knowledge Transfer

The Crusades (holy wars from 1095) brought thousands of Europeans into direct contact with Islamic medicine. Returning crusaders brought back medical knowledge, herbs, and surgical techniques far more advanced than anything in Europe. This was one of the key ways Islamic medical knowledge reached the West.

Usamah ibn Munqidh (1095–1188), a Muslim writer, recorded a striking story. An Arab doctor was treating a knight’s infected leg with clean dressings — and it was healing well. A European doctor arrived, dismissed the approach, and insisted on amputation. The knight died. The same European doctor then cut open a woman’s skull to treat her. She also died.

This story — told from a Muslim perspective — shows how far behind European surgery was compared to the Islamic world. It is useful evidence for exam answers about Islamic medicine’s contribution.

Religious encouragement: The Quran encouraged Muslims to seek knowledge and care for the sick — unlike the Christian Church’s focus on disease as God’s punishment.

Wealth and stability: The Islamic Empire was wealthy and stable. Rulers funded hospitals, libraries, and centres of learning. The great library at Baghdad, the House of Wisdom, attracted scholars from across the world.

Translation movement: Islamic scholars translated Greek and Roman texts into Arabic, preserving knowledge being lost in post-Roman Europe. They did not just copy these texts — they critiqued, corrected, and expanded them.

Practical emphasis: European medicine focused on theory and ancient authority. Islamic physicians placed greater emphasis on observation, experimentation, and practical results.

Key Individuals: A Timeline

c.854–925 AD

Rhazes (al-Razi)

Persian physician who first distinguished between smallpox and measles. Wrote over 200 medical texts and ran a hospital in Baghdad using clinical observation.

c.980–1037 AD

Ibn Sina (Avicenna)

Wrote The Canon of Medicine, a vast encyclopaedia used as Europe’s main medical textbook for over 500 years. Catalogued over 760 drugs.

c.1213–1288 AD

Ibn al-Nafis

Syrian physician who challenged Galen’s ideas about blood, correctly arguing that blood circulated through the lungs rather than passing through invisible pores in the heart. Anticipated Harvey by over 300 years.

By 1500

Over 1,200 hospitals in England

The Church had established a vast network of hospitals across medieval Britain, though their focus was on spiritual care rather than medical cure.

Your Site Question for 2027

AQA has named the Spanish Armada as the historic environment for your 2027 exam. That gives Paper 2 a guaranteed 16-mark question: a statement about the Armada, and the instruction to test it against a study of the site and your contextual knowledge. You already know the story of 1588 from Lesson 9. What this lesson adds is the site angle the examiner is actually paying for: the Armada as a journey through four environments — the Channel, the Calais anchorage, the waters off Gravelines, and the route home — each of which took its own toll.

Key Fact — Four Environments

Structure your site knowledge as four places: the Channel (a week of running battle), Calais (an exposed anchorage and fireships), Gravelines (gunnery and sandbanks), and the north-about route home (the storms that finished the fleet).

Environment One: The Channel

From the first sighting off Cornwall on 19 July 1588, warning beacons flashed the news along the coast, and the English fleet came out of Plymouth to begin a week-long running fight eastward. Two facts about this environment decided its character. First, the wind: the English worked themselves upwind of the Armada — the weather gauge — so every clash happened at a time and range of their choosing. Second, the shore: every port on that coast was English. Howard’s ships topped up powder, shot and food as they fought past their own harbours, while Medina Sidonia’s fleet had not one friendly quay between Spain and the Netherlands. The Armada’s crescent formation held together superbly all week — but it was a fleet holding its breath, spending supplies it could not replace.

Environment Two: Calais — the Anchorage With No Harbour

The plan required the Armada to collect the Duke of Parma’s invasion army from the Netherlands coast. But Spain controlled no deep-water port there: Parma’s barges sat in shallow harbours behind sandbanks, blockaded by Dutch flyboats, and needed days more to embark. So the Armada anchored in the open roadstead off Calais — a stretch of exposed water, not a harbour — because the map offered nothing better. The English answer took one night. Eight fireships came down the wind into the crowded anchorage, and the Spanish captains, unable to fight fire at anchor in the dark, cut their cables and ran. The formation that a week of cannon fire had failed to dent was scattered by the choice of anchorage — and every ship that cut its cable sailed for the rest of the campaign without its best anchors.

Environment Three: Gravelines and the Banks

Off Gravelines on 29 July, the English closed to effective gunnery range for the first time, battering the scattered Spanish ships while refusing the boarding fight the Armada was built for. Then geography nearly ended the campaign outright: the wind pressed the damaged fleet towards the Zeeland sandbanks, shoal water with no room to manoeuvre, and only a late change of wind let the Armada escape into the North Sea. That same wind shut the door behind it. With the English fleet between the Spanish and the Channel, the only route home was the long way — north around Scotland, west around Ireland.

A commemorative medal struck in the Protestant Netherlands credited the winds — God’s Protestant winds — with the victory, and English thanksgiving services made the same claim. It was brilliant propaganda, and about one-third true. The storms did destroy more ships than the navy did; but the fleet the storms caught had already been forced from its anchorage, stripped of its anchors, beaten at Gravelines and pushed onto the northern route by English action. In the site question, that layering — environment finishing what human choices began — is exactly the kind of judgement the top level rewards.

Environment Four: The Route Home

The north-about voyage was the deadliest environment of all. Autumn gales met a fleet with battle-damaged hulls, sick and starving crews, and — because of Calais — too few anchors to ride out storms off a lee shore. Wrecks piled up on the coasts of Scotland and, above all, western Ireland. Perhaps half the ships that left Spain never returned, and thousands of men died of drowning, hunger and disease — several times more than died to English guns. When Elizabeth delivered her famous speech at Tilbury on 9 August, the Armada was already limping into the North Sea; the environment spent the following weeks turning an English escape into a Spanish catastrophe.

Building Your 16-Mark Answer

Whatever the statement — about luck, leadership, weather, or English skill — answer it through feature-and-consequence chains drawn from the four environments: no deep-water port, therefore an exposed anchorage; an exposed anchorage, therefore fireships; cut cables, therefore wrecks on the Irish coast; English home ports and the weather gauge, therefore a fleet that could always refuse the fight the Spanish wanted. Then weigh in the human factors from Lesson 9 — the gunnery, the planning flaws, Parma’s blockaded barges — and reach a judgement. Site plus context, feature plus consequence: that is the whole recipe.

The Paradox of Progress

Modern public health is, in many ways, a victim of its own success. Vaccination, antibiotics, better sanitation, and the NHS have all extended life expectancy. But living longer has created new challenges. The diseases that dominate modern Britain are not the infectious epidemics of the past, but long-term degenerative conditions and illnesses linked to the way we live.

Key Fact

In 1900, average life expectancy in Britain was around 47 years. By 2020, it had risen to over 81 years. This extraordinary improvement is the result of centuries of medical progress — but it means today’s biggest health challenges are diseases of old age and lifestyle, not the infectious diseases that once killed millions.

New Diseases & Lifestyle Challenges

Long-Term Degenerative Conditions

As people live longer, the biggest medical challenges are conditions where the body slowly breaks down over time. These include:

  • Cancer — abnormal cell growth that can affect almost any part of the body. Risk increases significantly with age.
  • Alzheimer’s disease — a progressive brain disorder that destroys memory and cognitive function. It is the most common cause of dementia.
  • Parkinson’s disease — a condition affecting movement, causing tremors, stiffness, and difficulty with balance and coordination.

Lifestyle Diseases

Many of today’s most common illnesses are linked to modern lifestyles — poor diet, lack of exercise, smoking, and heavy drinking. These lifestyle diseases include:

  • Type 2 diabetes — strongly linked to obesity and poor diet. Cases have risen dramatically in recent decades.
  • Heart disease — the leading cause of death in the UK, linked to smoking, high-fat diets, and lack of exercise.
  • Some cancers — including lung cancer (linked to smoking), liver cancer (linked to alcohol), and bowel cancer (linked to processed meat and low-fibre diets).

Mental Health

Mental health is now one of the biggest public health challenges. Depression, anxiety, and eating disorders affect millions in Britain. Mental health services have always received less funding than physical health, despite affecting a similar number of people. Stigma has also made it harder for people to seek help, though awareness campaigns have begun to change this.

Antibiotic Resistance

One of the most serious global health threats today is antibiotic resistance. Decades of overusing antibiotics — in both human medicine and farming — have created superbugs: bacteria that have evolved to survive the drugs designed to kill them.

Key Fact

MRSA is one of the best-known superbugs. If antibiotic resistance continues to grow, routine operations like hip replacements, caesarean sections, and even dental surgery could become life-threatening because doctors would be unable to prevent or treat post-operative infections. The World Health Organization has called antibiotic resistance “one of the biggest threats to global health.”

Antibiotics have been overprescribed for decades — given for viral infections (where they have no effect), not finished by patients (letting partly resistant bacteria survive), and used routinely in farming to promote growth. Each time antibiotics are used wrongly, it gives bacteria a chance to evolve resistance.

At the same time, drug companies have invested less in new antibiotics because they are less profitable than drugs for long-term conditions. The result is a growing gap between resistant infections and the drugs available to treat them.

Challenges for the NHS

An Ageing Population

Britain’s population is ageing. Better healthcare and rising life expectancy mean more people are living into their 80s and 90s. This is a triumph of medical progress, but it puts huge pressure on the NHS. Older people are far more likely to have chronic conditions — heart disease, diabetes, dementia — that need expensive, ongoing care.

Key Fact

People aged 65 and over account for around 40% of NHS spending, despite making up less than 20% of the population. As the proportion of elderly people grows, the financial pressure on the NHS will only increase — raising difficult questions about how healthcare is funded and prioritised.

Rising Costs & Expectations

Modern medicine can achieve extraordinary things — but at huge cost. Treatments like chemotherapy, radiotherapy, robotic surgery, and gene therapy are all expensive. The NHS now costs around £201 billion per year to run. At the same time, public expectations have risen — people expect the latest treatments and shorter waiting times. Balancing demand against limited resources is one of the NHS’s greatest ongoing challenges.

Government Public Health Campaigns

Faced with rising lifestyle diseases, governments have used campaigns and laws to change behaviour and prevent illness. This continues the tradition of government action in public health that stretches back to the Public Health Acts of the nineteenth century.

Smoking bans: England banned smoking in enclosed public places in 2007. Smoking rates have fallen sharply, reducing lung cancer, heart disease, and respiratory illness.

Sugar tax: The 2018 Soft Drinks Industry Levy pushes manufacturers to cut sugar in drinks. It targets childhood obesity and type 2 diabetes.

Alcohol limits: Government campaigns promote lower recommended limits (14 units per week) to reduce liver disease, some cancers, and alcohol-related harm.

COVID-19 response: The COVID-19 pandemic (2020–2021) was the most dramatic government public health action in living memory. National lockdowns, mass testing, and the fastest vaccine rollout in history showed the scale of modern intervention — but also exposed inequalities in health outcomes based on income, ethnicity, and geography.

The Rise of Alternative Medicine & Skepticism

Despite huge advances in modern medicine, interest has grown in alternative medicine — treatments like acupuncture, aromatherapy, homeopathy, and hypnotherapy that sit outside mainstream evidence-based medicine. Some people turn to these when conventional medicine cannot cure their condition, or because they prefer a more “natural” approach.

Vaccine Skepticism

A more dangerous trend is growing vaccine skepticism. In 1998, Andrew Wakefield published a fraudulent study claiming the MMR vaccine caused autism. The study was later thoroughly discredited — Wakefield was struck off the medical register and the paper was retracted — but the damage was done. Vaccination rates dropped, and measles — almost eliminated — began to return.

Key Fact

The MMR scare is a powerful example of how misinformation can undermine public health. Lower vaccination rates in some areas led to outbreaks of measles — a preventable disease. It demonstrates that public health progress is never permanent and can be reversed by loss of public trust.

The Thalidomide Disaster

Key Fact

The thalidomide disaster is one of modern medicine’s most important warnings. In the late 1950s, thalidomide was prescribed to pregnant women for morning sickness. It caused severe birth defects — thousands of babies were born with shortened or missing limbs. The scandal led to much stricter drug testing and regulation, and is a stark reminder that thorough testing is essential before treatments reach patients.

Genetic Medicine & DNA

One of the most exciting areas of modern medicine is genetic medicine — using knowledge of DNA and genes to prevent, diagnose, and treat disease. This field has been transformed by the Human Genome Project.

1953

Watson and Crick discover the structure of DNA

James Watson and Francis Crick (building on Rosalind Franklin’s X-ray work) identify the double-helix structure of DNA, the molecule that carries genetic instructions for all living things.

1990–2003

The Human Genome Project

An international project to map the entire human genetic code. It identified approximately 20,000–25,000 human genes and created the foundation for genetic medicine.

2000s onwards

Gene therapy trials begin

Gene therapy — replacing or repairing faulty genes to treat disease — enters clinical trials for conditions including certain cancers, inherited blindness, and blood disorders.

Present day

Personalised medicine

Personalised medicine allows treatments to be tailored to a patient’s individual genetic profile. Cancer patients, for example, can have their tumour’s DNA analysed to find the most effective drug for their specific type.

Key Fact — Genetic Testing in Practice

In 2013, actress Angelina Jolie publicly announced that genetic testing had revealed she carried a mutated BRCA1 gene, giving her a very high risk of developing breast cancer — her mother, grandmother, and aunt had all died of cancer. She chose to have a preventative double mastectomy to reduce her risk. This high-profile case showed how DNA knowledge can now allow people to take preventative action against diseases they have not yet developed — a revolutionary shift from treating illness after it appears to preventing it before it begins.

Genetic medicine fits into the broader course narrative. Just as Jenner’s vaccination, Pasteur’s germ theory, and Fleming’s penicillin each changed everything, genetic medicine could transform twenty-first century healthcare. It also raises ethical questions about privacy, cost, and access — echoing debates about the NHS and public health throughout the course.

Examiners increasingly expect students to show awareness of modern developments and connect them to broader themes — especially the role of science and technology in medical change.
